title: A meta-analysis of humor in advertising
venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
finding: Meta-analysis of humour effects in advertising; the OpenAlex record carries no abstract, only keywords (attention, brand recall, brand attitude, purchase intention, positive affect, source credibility), so no effect sizes can be quoted from this session.
why_for_us: The anchor meta-analysis for humour in ads; read the full text before quoting any number to the team about humour raising attention vs. credibility.

title: How humor in advertising works: A meta-analytic test of alternative models
finding: Meta-analytic test of competing cognitive vs. affective models of how ad humour works; the OpenAlex record has no abstract (keywords: counterargument, cognitive effort, positive affect, congruency effect), so model results cannot be quoted here.
why_for_us: Relevant to whether the Komputerku gag persuades by mood or by lowering counterarguing; check full text before relying on it.

title: The Impact of Humor in Advertising: A Review
finding: Narrative review: later research only partially supports earlier conclusions; humour is no guarantee of better ads and its effect depends on the objective, audience, situation and type of humour, per authors.
why_for_us: Decide first what each episode must achieve (awareness of the brand vs. understanding of drafting accuracy) and choose humour type for that goal and for a notary audience.

title: Assessing the Use and Impact of Humor on Advertising Effectiveness: A Contingency Approach
finding: Content analysis of print ads by humour mechanism, intentional relatedness of humour to the product, and product group: the dominant practice (incongruity humour in a humour-dominant ad) may not be the most effective for ad performance across product groups, per authors.
why_for_us: Humour should be intentionally related to the product (the drafting tool itself), not a humour-dominant sketch that just happens to end with a logo.

title: Humour effect on memory and attitude: moderating role of product involvement
finding: Field data (multi-year Super Bowl ad survey 1992-1997, regression): humorous ads were positively related to memory and attitude toward the ad, and the advantage was larger for low-involvement products, per authors.
why_for_us: Legal-practice software is a high-involvement, high-risk purchase, so expect a smaller humour bonus than for snacks; humour should open the door, substance must close it.

title: The Impact of Perceived Humor, Product Type, and Humor Style in Radio Advertising
venue: Journal of Current Issues & Research in Advertising
finding: Experiment with radio ads (incongruity vs. incongruity-resolution, higher vs. lower risk products): perceived humorousness overwhelmed humour type and product risk; ads only helped attitude to ad and brand if perceived as funny, and failed humour carries risk, per authors.
why_for_us: Pretest each episode with real notaries and staff: a joke that does not land is worse than no joke, regardless of how 'serious' the product is.

title: Humor in Advertising: The Moderating Role of Prior Brand Evaluation
finding: Experiment: with positive prior brand evaluation a humorous ad beat a non-humorous one on attitude change and choice; with negative prior evaluation the humorous ad was less effective than the non-humorous one, per authors.
why_for_us: For notaries already sceptical of AI drafting tools, heavy humour may backfire; use lighter humour for cold audiences and the running gag for warm followers/existing users.

title: Exploring memory for product names advertised with humour
finding: Three experiments: humour impaired memory for products but enhanced memory for the ads; humorously promoted brands were less accessible in memory; one week later the effect was in conscious recall only, unconscious familiarity unaffected, per authors.
why_for_us: Risk that viewers remember 'the little computer that eats credits' but not the product name; tie the brand name into the gag and repeat it on screen.

title: Humor in advertisements enhances product liking by mere association.
finding: Experiments: products repeatedly paired with humorous (vs. non-humorous) cartoons in a mock magazine gained more liking through implicit attitude change, which also predicted product choice, per authors.
why_for_us: Even if the brand is not consciously recalled, warm association with the product can build; keep product visibly present during the funny moments.

title: The Influence of Humor Strength and Humor—Message Relatedness on Ad Memorability: A Dual Process Model
finding: Experiments: ads were most memorable when humour was both strong and related to the message; the interaction was mediated by attention and mood; strong humour also raised recall among people high in need for humour, per authors.
why_for_us: The 'feeding the computer' gag works best if it is about the actual product mechanics (credits, drafting), not an unrelated joke.

title: Humor and ad memorability: On the contributions of humor expectancy, relevancy, and need for humor
finding: Experiment: message claims recall was damaged when humour was expected, especially when the expected humour was related to the message; need for humour moderated effects, per authors.
why_for_us: In a running series viewers come to expect the gag; vary its form so the claim (time saved, accuracy) is not lost in an anticipated punchline.

title: Humor and Advertising Effectiveness after Repeated Exposures to a Radio Commercial
finding: Experiment with repeated exposure to a radio ad: adding humour to a hierarchy-of-effects model did not improve overall explanatory power; humour perceived after repeated exposures was linked to effectiveness measures (abstract truncated before direction for each outcome), per authors.
why_for_us: Wear-out matters for a series: plan how the running gag evolves across 60-90 s episodes rather than repeating the same joke.

title: Explaining variations in the use of humor in advertising across countries: a meta-analysis
finding: Meta-analysis of content analyses across 15 countries over 90 years plus an experiment: humour is used more in advertising in countries where relationships are more negotiable (more potential mate-seekers), and activating mate-seeking increased humour use, per authors.
why_for_us: Prevalence of ad humour is culture-dependent (Polish co-authors); do not assume US/UK ad-humour norms transfer to Polish notaries without local testing.

title: Risky Business: When Humor Increases and Decreases Status
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: Eight experiments: successful humour raised status in new and existing relationships, mediated by perceived confidence and competence; failed or inappropriate jokes signalled confidence but low competence and harmed status, per authors.
why_for_us: For a status-conscious profession the notary character must 'win' through humour (competent, in control), never look foolish; an inappropriate joke costs the brand perceived competence.

title: Gender and the evaluation of humor at work.
finding: Experiment (N=216): humorous men were ascribed higher status than non-humorous men, while humorous women were ascribed lower status than non-humorous women, with downstream effects on performance evaluations and perceived leadership capability, per authors.
why_for_us: Many notaries and most office staff in Poland are women; avoid making a female notary the joke-teller whose authority depends on the gag - let situations or the computer carry the humour.

title: Laughing and liking: Exploring the interpersonal effects of humor use in initial social interactions
finding: Two interaction experiments with unacquainted dyads: humour was positively associated with liking and closeness, mediated by perceived reciprocal liking and enjoyment; no sex difference in self-reported humour use, per authors.
why_for_us: Shared laughter builds liking with a new audience; useful for first-contact episodes before any product pitch.

title: The relationship between leader self-deprecating humor and perceived effectiveness: Trust in leader as a mediator
finding: Three cross-sectional samples (regression, bootstrapping): leader self-deprecating humour positively related to perceived leader effectiveness, partly mediated by trust in the leader; single-source, non-causal design, per authors.
why_for_us: A senior notary laughing gently at his own tech clumsiness can build trust, provided his legal competence is never the target.

title: “It's not you, it's me”: transformational leadership and self‐deprecating humor
finding: Experiment (N=155 undergraduates, four humour conditions in a leader speech): leaders using self-deprecating humour were rated higher on individualized consideration than leaders using aggressive humour, per authors.
why_for_us: Self-deprecation narrows status gaps; aggressive humour (mocking assistants or clients) widens them - keep the boss-notary self-targeted.

title: Does leader humor style matter and to whom?
finding: Field survey of 428 employee-supervisor dyads in 19 service organisations: affiliative and self-enhancing leader humour helped low core-self-evaluation employees build trust and performance; aggressive leader humour reduced performance via lower trust regardless of employee traits, per authors.
why_for_us: Affiliative humour (laughing with the team) is the safe register for depicting a notary office; aggressive humour erodes trust.

title: The use of disparaging humor by group leaders
finding: Experiment: a leader using self-disparaging humour was seen as better at relieving tension and encouraging participation; superior-targeted humour lowered ratings of helpfulness and willingness to share opinions; subordinate-targeted humour also had costs (abstract truncated), per authors.
why_for_us: Direction of the joke matters: target the machine or oneself, not the trainee or the client.

title: A meta‐analysis of positive humor in the workplace
finding: Meta-analysis (k=49, N=8,532): employee humour associated with better performance, satisfaction, workgroup cohesion, health and coping, and lower burnout, stress and withdrawal; supervisor humour associated with better subordinate performance, satisfaction, perceived supervisor performance and cohesion; authors warn derogatory or sexist humour raises legal concerns.
why_for_us: Gives a credible frame: showing a notary office that laughs together is aspirational (cohesive, less burned out), not unprofessional - as long as humour is positive.

title: The state of research on leader humor
finding: Systematic review with meta-analysis and path analyses of leader humour: documents links to leadership effectiveness but flags construct-clarity and measurement problems (trait humour vs. humour expression); effect sizes not stated in the abstract.
why_for_us: Leader humour evidence is real but measurement is messy; do not overclaim when citing it in sales material.

title: Are Positive and Negative Leader Humor Two Different Coins? A Meta-analysis
finding: Meta-analysis of positive vs. negative leader humour and their nomological network (keywords: positive/negative affect, leader-member exchange, innovation, OCB); the OpenAlex record has no abstract, so no effect sizes can be quoted here.
why_for_us: Newest synthesis on whether negative leader humour is distinct from positive; read full text before citing.

title: How fun are your meetings? Investigating the relationship between humor patterns in team interactions and team performance.
finding: Field data: 54 videotaped real team meetings; humour patterns (joke-laughter-joke) triggered positive socio-emotional talk, procedural structure and new solutions and predicted team performance immediately and two years later, but only in low job-insecurity climates; humour or laughter alone did not, per authors.
why_for_us: Show reciprocal humour among staff, not a lone joker; and note that where staff fear AI will replace them (job insecurity) humour loses its benefit - address that fear directly.

title: Is humor the best medicine? The buffering effect of coping humor on traumatic stressors in firefighters
finding: Two-wave survey of 179 firefighters: traumatic events predicted burnout, PTSD and absenteeism, and coping humour buffered the link for burnout and PTSD, per authors.
why_for_us: Humour as coping with pressure is legitimate in serious professions; a notary office under deadline pressure laughing it off is credible.

title: Whatever Gets You Through Today: An Examination of Cynical Humor Among Emergency Service Professionals
finding: Literature review: black/gallows humour is almost universally used by emergency personnel and serves venting, group cohesion and emotional distancing that lets them act effectively, per authors.
why_for_us: Insider humour of a profession is a bonding tool, but it is meant for insiders; jokes that work in the back office may read as callous when shown to clients.

title: Humour in business: A double-edged sword
finding: Discourse study of humour in business meetings (record has no abstract; keywords: formality, solidarity, power, in-group, exclusion, collusion, inclusion), framing humour as both including and excluding.
why_for_us: Humour can bond the in-group (notaries) and exclude outsiders (clients, juniors); decide who is 'in' on each joke.

title: Lawyers' use of humor as persuasion
venue: Humor - International Journal of Humor Research
finding: Discourse analysis of US court-mandated mediation and Supreme Court oral argument: attorneys used humour aggressively to ridicule opposing claims as laughable while showcasing their own verbal skill; humour and wordplay are valued as evidence of forensic skill in the US system, per author.
why_for_us: Legal professionals do prize wit as a sign of skill - but as sharp, verbal, competence-displaying humour, not slapstick; the notary character should be the clever one.

title: Taking Laughter Seriously at the Supreme Court
finding: Field data: over 9,000 laughter events in US Supreme Court oral arguments since 1955; Justices use humour as advocacy and a signal of power and status, aiming it mostly at advocates they disagree with, who are losing, or who are novices; laughter helps predict votes, per authors.
why_for_us: In legal hierarchies humour flows downward and marks status; jokes in the series should never put the notary in the position of the laughed-at novice.

title: Banter from the Bench: The Use of Humour in the Exercise of Judicial Functions
finding: Legal analysis: most Australian judicial officers exercise caution and restraint with humour; arguments for it (humanity, demystifying ritual, easing tension, gentle admonishment) are weighed against duties of independence and propriety and risk of apprehended bias or complaints; authors conclude humour has a place within judicial discretion.
why_for_us: Mirrors the notarial ethos: humour is tolerated when it eases tension and demystifies, not when it undermines the dignity of the office - keep the notary's official act (signing, reading the deed) outside the joke.

title: Humour in the Swedish Court: Managing Emotions, Status and Power
finding: Book chapter on humour among Swedish judges and prosecutors (no abstract in record; keywords: emotional management, status, power, group solidarity, shame management, interprofessional relations) - a civil-law court setting.
why_for_us: Closest civil-law analogue found to notarial practice: humour there serves backstage solidarity and emotion management among professionals.

title: “You must be joking”: the role of humour in the law classroom
finding: Conceptual article: evidence on humour in law teaching is mostly anecdotal; drawing on 'difficult subject' literature, authors set out benefits (relaxed climate, motivation, engagement) and pitfalls and illustrate appropriate humour in law teaching.
why_for_us: Lawyers were trained in environments where humour was rare and anecdotal; explanatory humour around a difficult topic (drafting rules) is the form they have seen work.

title: Lowering the Bar: Lawyer Jokes and Legal Culture
finding: Book by Galanter analysing the genre of American lawyer jokes and their relation to legal culture (no abstract in the OpenAlex book record).
why_for_us: Background on how the profession is mocked from outside; the series should not import hostile 'lawyer joke' tropes (greed, lies) about notaries.

title: Physician-Patient Communication The Relationship With Malpractice Claims Among Primary Care Physicians and Surgeons
finding: Field data (audiotapes of 10 routine visits each from 59 primary care physicians and 65 surgeons): no-claims primary care physicians laughed and used humour more, oriented and facilitated more, and had longer visits (18.3 vs 15.0 min) than claims physicians; the model improved prediction of claims by 57% above chance; no such differences for surgeons, per authors.
why_for_us: In a trust-heavy professional service, light humour is part of a relationship that keeps clients from complaining; depicting notary-client warmth is credible, but effects may be specialty-specific.

title: Satisfaction and the Use of Humor by Physicians and Patients
finding: Coded 92 audiotaped primary care visits (half high, half low satisfaction): high-satisfaction visits had more light, tension-relieving, self-effacing and positive-function humour from both physicians and patients, per authors.
why_for_us: Light, tension-relieving, self-effacing humour is the type professional-service clients reward; model the client scenes on that.

title: Increasing patient satisfaction and compliance: An examination of physician humor orientation, compliance‐gaining strategies, and perceived credibility
finding: Survey (N=184 across four samples): perceived physician humour orientation was positively related to perceived physician credibility, patient satisfaction and compliance, per authors; correlational.
why_for_us: Correlational support that humour and credibility can coexist for experts; the notary in the series can be funny and credible.

title: To humor or not humor buyers? Evaluating the effective use of humor in B2B advertisements
finding: The OpenAlex record has no abstract; keywords indicate a test of humour in B2B ads on attitude toward the ad, brand attitude, supplier relationships and information-seeking intention via serial mediation. Direction and size of effects cannot be quoted from this session.
why_for_us: The most on-point study for selling to professional buyers; obtain the full text before deciding how much humour the notary campaign can carry.

title: The effects of humor usage by salespersons: the roles of humor type and business sector
venue: Journal of Business and Industrial Marketing
finding: Survey of 175 B2B salespersons: constructive humour related positively to relationship quality and business performance across sectors; offensive humour related negatively, but only in non-service-based sectors, per authors; single-country, self-report.
why_for_us: Constructive humour is safe in B2B selling; for a professional-service buyer keep it constructive and never offensive.

title: The role of humor usage on creativity, trust and performance in business relationships: An analysis of the salesperson-customer dyad
finding: The OpenAlex record has no abstract; keywords indicate a salesperson-customer dyad study linking humour usage to customer trust, sales performance and relational continuity. No effect sizes available here.
why_for_us: Suggests humour is part of trust-building in B2B relationships; check full text for direction of effects before citing.

title: Using different advertising humor appeals to generate firm-level warmth and competence impressions
venue: International Journal of Research in Marketing
finding: The OpenAlex record has no abstract; keywords indicate that different humour appeals (incongruity-resolution vs. tension relief) are tested for firm-level warmth and competence impressions. Results cannot be quoted here.
why_for_us: Directly about whether humour makes a firm look warm but incompetent, the key risk for a legal-tech vendor; high-priority full-text read.

title: Effects of Humor in Task-Oriented Human-Computer Interaction and Computer-Mediated Communication: A Direct Test of SRCT Theory
finding: Two between-subjects experiments (humour vs. control comments): humour raised likability, cooperation and perceived similarity of the partner without changing task time or effort; when participants believed the partner was a computer, effects were similar but weaker (less sociability, less mirth, less similarity), per authors.
why_for_us: A joking computer does not make users work less seriously; a little personality in 'Komputerku' can raise likability without implying the tool is frivolous.

title: The effect of voice and humour on users’ perceptions of personal intelligent agents
finding: Online experiment: humour and voice increased perceived anthropomorphism of a personal intelligent agent, which raised emotion-based trust and intention to use; cognitive-based trust was driven by perceived intelligence, not humour, per authors.
why_for_us: Humour makes the 'little computer' feel human and likable (emotional trust), but competence trust must come from showing it draft correctly - pair every gag with proof of intelligence.

title: Use of humor by a healthcare robot positively affects user perceptions and behavior.
finding: Experiment (N=91, humorous vs. neutral robot in a flu-vaccination scenario): the humorous robot was rated more likeable, safer, more empathic and sociable, but also more 'frivolous'; more participants laughed, per authors.
why_for_us: Even in a serious setting a humorous machine is liked more, but the 'frivolous' side effect is a warning for a product that must look reliable with legal documents.

title: Chatbots in complaint handling: the moderating role of humor
venue: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management
finding: Two scenario experiments: perceived control and social presence both improved chatbot complaint handling; humorous chatbot language weakened the benefit of perceived control but strengthened the benefit of social presence, per authors.
why_for_us: When the product message is 'you stay in control of the deed', humour may dilute it; use humour for the relationship moments, keep control/accuracy moments straight.

title: A Review of Humor in Educational Settings: Four Decades of Research
finding: Narrative review of four decades of classroom humour research: definitions, functions and theories, types of instructional humour, source and receiver findings, with emphasis on explaining inconsistent results; abstract gives no effect sizes.
why_for_us: Standard reference for 'humour that teaches'; useful for episodes that explain a drafting feature.

title: Teaching and Learning with Humor: Experiment and Replication
finding: Two semester-long field experiments (N=161 statistics students; replication N=132 psychology students): classes taught with relevant humour scored significantly higher on the final exam than no-humour classes taught by the same teacher, per author.
why_for_us: Relevant humour improves retention of serious content over weeks; the gag should be built on the feature being taught.

title: An Explanation of the Relationship between Instructor Humor and Student Learning: Instructional Humor Processing Theory
finding: Survey (N=378 students): content-related humour was positively associated with student learning, while other-disparaging and offensive humour did not correlate with learning; proposes Instructional Humor Processing Theory (incongruity resolution + disposition + ELM), per authors.
why_for_us: Related humour helps learning; disparaging humour adds nothing - again, the joke must be about the product task, not at someone's expense.

title: Exploratory Theoretical Tests of the Instructor Humor–Student Learning Link
finding: Survey (N=300): instructional humour processing theory did not adequately explain the humour-perceived cognitive learning link; self-determination theory (humour supporting autonomy/engagement) fitted better, per authors.
why_for_us: Humour may work on professionals by making learning feel self-chosen and engaging, not just by attention; contradicts the simple IHPT story.

title: Effects of humor on sentence memory.
venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology Learning Memory and Cognition
finding: Experiments: humorous sentences were better remembered than non-humorous versions on free and cued recall; effects persisted with warning but were attenuated in incidental learning and limited to within-subjects designs; humorous material receives more attention and rehearsal, per author.
why_for_us: Humour aids memory mainly relative to surrounding non-humorous content - the funny line wins at the expense of neighbours, so put the key product claim inside the funny line.

title: The impact of humor on memory: Is the humor effect about humor?
venue: Humor - International Journal of Humor Research
finding: Experiment comparing semantic elaboration, incongruity resolution and perceived humour explanations: participants' humour ratings predicted recall even controlling for elaboration and incongruity resolution, per author.
why_for_us: Only content that the audience actually finds funny gets the memory boost; test with notaries, not with the creative team.

title: Humor in the Eye Tracker: Attention Capture and Distraction from Context Cues
finding: Eye-tracking experiment: humorous texts paired with novel brands received prolonged attention relative to positive and neutral texts, and this enhanced attention correlated with impaired brand recognition, per authors.
why_for_us: Mechanism for brand-name loss: the joke steals the eyes; put the logo/name inside the joke frame, not next to it.

title: Use of humour in medical education: a survey of students and teachers at a medical school in China
finding: Cross-sectional surveys (327 medical students, 165 physician teachers): 87% agreed with using humour in teaching; interesting clinical cases were the most used and most effective humour type; lack of subject-related humorous material was the main barrier, per authors.
why_for_us: Professionals in serious fields welcome humour that comes from real cases; build gags from real notarial office situations rather than generic jokes.

title: When Does Humorous Marketing Hurt Brands?
finding: Three experiments and one correlational study: humorous marketing more likely hurt brand attitudes when the ad was highly (vs. mildly) threatening, made fun of a subset of the population rather than people in general, and motivated avoidance rather than approach - even when consumers found it funny, per authors.
why_for_us: Never make the joke at the expense of a subgroup (older notaries, assistants, clients); keep the 'threat' mild (a hungry computer, not a lost deed).

title: Being funny is not enough: the influence of perceived humor and negative emotional reactions on brand attitudes
finding: Four samples of real advertisements: brand attitudes depended less on how funny the ad seemed and more on how much negative emotion it triggered; whether an ad helps or hurts depends on whether it raises or lowers negative feelings independent of perceived humour, per authors.
why_for_us: Screen every episode for discomfort (embarrassment of the notary, mocking of staff, fear about errors in deeds), not just for laughs; a funny but uncomfortable episode can still hurt the brand.

title: The joint impact of humor and argument strength in a print advertising context: A case for weaker arguments
finding: Lab experiment with print ads for a convenience good: incidental humour produced more positive attitudes when arguments were weak but less positive attitudes when arguments were strong, per authors.
why_for_us: If the product has strong arguments (hours saved, fewer drafting errors), heavy incidental humour can undercut them; let strong claims be stated plainly and keep the gag around, not over, them.

title: It’s no laughing matter: An exploratory study of the use of ironic versus sarcastic humor in health-related advertising messages
finding: Experiment (N=303): sarcastic messages vs. no humour produced less negative affect but more counterarguing and lower perceived argument strength; ironic messages also increased counterarguing; counterarguing mediated effects on attitudes, per authors.
why_for_us: Sarcasm about the 'old way' of drafting may trigger resistance among notaries who still work that way; prefer warm irony at the machine over sarcasm at the viewer.

title: Egocentrism over e-mail: Can we communicate as well as we think?
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: Five experiments: people overestimate how well they convey tone (e.g. sarcasm or humour) in e-mail, due to egocentrism - senders 'hear' their intended tone that receivers do not, per authors.
why_for_us: Captions, LinkedIn posts and subtitles of the series lose intonation; deadpan or sarcastic lines may be read literally by notaries scrolling without sound - signal the joke visually.

title: Age-related differences in judgments of inappropriate behavior are related to humor style preferences.
finding: Experiment with young, middle-aged and older adults: all discriminated appropriate from inappropriate behaviour equally, but only young and middle-aged adults found social-gaffe clips funnier; young adults endorsed more aggressive humour, which mediated age differences, per authors.
why_for_us: Cringe/gaffe comedy that works for younger staff may fall flat with senior notaries; test episodes across age groups.

title: Humor and Aging - A Mini-Review
finding: Mini-review: older people appear to enjoy humour more but have more difficulty understanding jokes, laugh less, enjoy aggressive humour less and are especially sensitive to jokes about old age; mostly cross-sectional studies with possible cohort effects, per author.
why_for_us: Avoid age jokes and complex layered punchlines for the senior-notary segment; keep incongruities simple and resolvable.
